title: Left Out of a Game of Catch
text:
The psychologist Kipling Williams once found himself in a park, tossed a frisbee by two strangers who then went back to throwing it only to each other. He was surprised how bad it felt to be left out, and he turned the experience into a simple computer game called Cyberball, in which a player tosses a virtual ball with two others on screen.

In 2003 Naomi Eisenberger and Matthew Lieberman of the University of California, Los Angeles, together with Williams, used the game in a brain scanner. Each participant believed they were playing online with two other people, though the other players were run by the computer. In one round, the participant could only watch, supposedly because of a technical problem. In another, the participant was included in the game for a few throws, and then the two others threw the ball only to each other for the rest of the round.

Being excluded by strangers in a meaningless game left people feeling distressed and ignored, as they reported afterward. The brain scans showed increased activity in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, a region also involved in the distress of physical pain, and the more upset people felt, the more active it was. Social rejection, the researchers suggested, may draw on some of the same alarm systems as bodily pain.
lesson: Even small exclusions hurt. Notice who is being left out of the conversation, the meeting or the game, and throw them the ball.
people: Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman, Kipling Williams
location: University of California, Los Angeles, USA
source: Eisenberger, N. I., Lieberman, M. D., and Williams, K. D. (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion. Science, 302(5643), 290-292.
caveat: The brain imaging study was small, and the claim that social pain and physical pain share the same brain systems is debated, though the distress caused by exclusion is well replicated.
